bodyHtml:
1.1 Terminology Glossary

Why This Matters

Trading starts to feel confusing when new words arrive faster than understanding. The fix is not to memorize everything at once. The fix is to sort each word into the job it does.

This lesson uses a simple rule:

  • price words tell you what the market is doing now;
  • product words tell you what you are trading;
  • account words tell you how much money and risk are involved.

If you can sort the vocabulary correctly, later lessons become much easier.

What You Should Understand After This Lesson

By the end of this lesson, you should be able to:

  • explain the difference between terms like pip, tick, margin, and equity;
  • tell whether a word is about price, the product, or the trading account;
  • avoid the most common beginner vocabulary mistakes.

The Three Main Buckets

1. Price Words

These words describe the live market price and how it moves.

Term Plain-English meaning
Bid The price a buyer is willing to pay right now.
Ask The price a seller is willing to accept right now.
Spread The gap between the bid and the ask.
Pip A common FX movement unit.
Tick The smallest allowed price move in many exchange-traded contracts.
Point A larger price move, often used for indices and futures.

(Table alt-text: A simple glossary table showing six price-related terms and one-sentence beginner definitions for each.)

2. Product Words

These words describe what kind of thing you are trading.

Term Plain-English meaning
Spot Trading the market price for near-immediate settlement.
Futures Standardized contracts that settle later under exchange rules.
Option A contract that gives a right, but not an obligation, to buy or sell at a set price.
Strike The set price written into an option contract.
Premium The price paid for an option contract.
Expiry The date when a futures or options contract ends.

(Table alt-text: A glossary table showing six product-related trading terms and clear beginner explanations.)

3. Account Words

These words describe your money, exposure, and trading capacity.

Term Plain-English meaning
Margin Money set aside as collateral for a leveraged position.
Leverage Using a small amount of money to control a larger position.
Balance The money in your account after closed trades and cash movements are counted.
Equity Your balance plus or minus the result of open trades.
Free Margin Money not currently tied up in open positions.
Floating P/L Profit or loss on a trade that is still open.

(Table alt-text: A glossary table showing six account-related trading terms and beginner-friendly definitions.)

One Very Simple Price Example

Imagine EUR/USD is showing:

  • Bid: 1.0850
  • Ask: 1.0851

That means:

  • you buy at the ask;
  • you sell at the bid;
  • the spread is 1 pip.

If you buy and then instantly close the trade, you do not start at zero. You start slightly negative because the spread is a cost.

This same idea exists in many markets, even if the movement unit changes from pips to ticks or points.

Margin and Leverage in Plain English

These two words are related, but they are not the same.

  • Leverage is the bigger exposure.
  • Margin is the money held to support that exposure.

A simple way to think about it:

  • leverage is the size of the position;
  • margin is the security deposit that helps hold that position open.

This matters because beginners often hear “I used 10x leverage” and think it means more opportunity. It also means losses can grow faster.

Balance, Equity, and Floating P/L

These words describe different views of your account.

Example:

  • Account balance: $1,000
  • One open trade is down: $80

Then:

  • Balance is still $1,000 because the trade is not closed yet.
  • Floating P/L is -$80.
  • Equity is $920 because it includes the open loss.

If the trade later closes at that loss, the balance will then fall to $920.

Why Units Can Mislead You

If someone says, “The market moved 20,” that sentence is incomplete.

It could mean:

  • 20 pips in a currency pair;
  • 20 ticks in a futures contract;
  • 20 points in an index;
  • 20 cents in a commodity.

Those are not equal in money terms.

Global example:

  • In EUR/USD, traders often speak in pips.
  • In Nikkei futures, traders often need to think in points or ticks depending on the contract.
  • In Brent crude, the cash effect depends on the contract and the price increment used by the venue.

The safe question is always:

20 what?

Common Beginner Mistakes

Mistake 1: Thinking Margin and Leverage Mean the Same Thing

They are connected, but they describe different things. Margin is collateral. Leverage is amplified exposure.

Mistake 2: Thinking Balance and Equity Always Match

They only match when there are no open trades affecting the account.

Mistake 3: Thinking a Pip, Tick, and Point Are Interchangeable

They are all movement units, but they do not mean the same cash value.

Mistake 4: Thinking Spot, Futures, and Options Are Just Three Names for Trading

They are different product structures with different rules.
learningOutcomes: explain the difference between common trading terms that are often confused by beginners;
identify when a term changes meaning across asset classes;
read basic product descriptions without mistaking vocabulary for strategy.

quizItems.prompt: Which term describes the collateral required to support leveraged exposure?
quizItems.explanation: Margin is collateral. Leverage is the amplified exposure created from using that collateral.

quizItems.prompt: Which price increment is most commonly used to describe many FX pair movements?
quizItems.explanation: A pip is a common FX price increment, while a tick is the minimum price increment on many exchange-traded contracts.

quizItems.prompt: What is the best plain-English description of equity?

choices.label: C
choices.text: Balance adjusted for open profit and loss

correctAnswer.label: C
correctAnswer.text: Balance adjusted for open profit and loss

quizItems.explanation: Equity changes with open positions. Balance usually reflects realized results and cash movements.
